overview: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines became independent in 1979. This geographic history includes the earlier Kalinago and Garifuna presence, colonial rule and struggles over land and labour. Indigenous village remains, farming practices and community knowledge reveal lives beyond changes of government.

periods.title: An Indigenous village at Argyle
periods.summary: Excavation at Argyle identified a sixteenth-century village with house plans and both Indigenous and European objects. This is evidence for a particular settlement and its connections.

periods.title: Britain claims Saint Vincent by treaty
periods.summary: The Treaty of Paris assigned Saint Vincent to Britain. An agreement between imperial powers did not establish Indigenous consent to British occupation.

periods.title: A treaty after the First Carib War
periods.summary: The treaty required recognition of British sovereignty while setting aside territory for Indigenous communities. Conflict over land persisted.

periods.title: French capture with Garifuna allies
periods.summary: French forces and their Garifuna allies took the island from Britain in 1779.

periods.title: British colonial control resumes
periods.summary: The 1783 peace settlement returned Saint Vincent to Britain, part of a wider redistribution of Caribbean colonies.

periods.title: War, defeat and confinement
periods.summary: Chatoyer died during the war begun in 1795. British victory led to confinement on Balliceaux, where disease and inadequate supplies killed many captives.

periods.title: Forced exile to Roatán
periods.summary: Britain deported Garifuna survivors to Roatán in 1797. Communities subsequently established lives along the Central American coast while maintaining connections with Saint Vincent.

periods.title: Abolition and compulsory apprenticeship
periods.summary: Abolition in 1834 was followed by compulsory apprenticeship intended to bind workers to former enslavers. Repression continued on the estates.

periods.title: Apprenticeship ends
periods.summary: The system ended in 1838. Many women left estate work to cultivate and market food crops, seeking greater control over their livelihoods.

periods.title: Adult suffrage and ministerial government
periods.summary: The 1951 constitution extended voting rights to adults aged twenty-one and over. A ministerial system followed in 1956.

periods.title: Internal self-government
periods.summary: Associated statehood began on 27 October 1969. Britain retained defence and external affairs while Saint Vincent governed its internal affairs.

periods.title: An independent state
periods.summary: Independence began on 27 October 1979 under the name Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. The new constitution replaced the associated-state arrangements.

periods.title: La Soufrière erupts
periods.summary: Lava emerged in December 2020, followed by explosions in April 2021. Monitoring and communication supported evacuation before the explosive phase.

periods.title: Communities document recovery
periods.summary: An exhibition shared residents’ photographs of returning to northern communities after the eruption, alongside participation in rainfall monitoring.

sections.title: Discoveries, buildings and a surviving object

items.text: At Argyle, archaeologists recovered the plans of eleven houses. Two larger elongated structures were interpreted as men’s houses through comparison with Raymond Breton’s historical descriptions. The excavated outlines provide evidence of building arrangements; their proposed social functions depend on interpretation as well as the physical remains.

The village also yielded pottery, beads, axe heads and European wares. Ceramic connections extend toward South America and the Greater Antilles. Reconstruction involved local experts and Kalinago and Garifuna participants in choices about wood, binding and roofing, bringing archaeological evidence into discussion with living building knowledge.

A carved coconut-shell ladle in the West India Committee collection bears Chatoyer’s name and the date 1773 on a silver rim. Its exact provenance is unknown, and its handle may be a later addition. Association with a diplomatic gift is plausible, not proven by the inscription alone.

sections.title: Land, forced migration and continuing communities

items.text: The 1763 treaty speaks in the language of possession by crowns. Saint Vincent’s Indigenous inhabitants were not parties to that agreement. The treaty therefore documents an imperial claim, while later negotiations and wars show that control on the ground remained contested.

The Garifuna Heritage Foundation connects the forced exile of 1797 with communities in Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua. Its account also stresses enduring ties with people on Saint Vincent. Deportation was a catastrophic loss of homeland and autonomy, followed by cultural survival across new places.

UNESCO’s recognition concerns Garifuna language, dance and music in Central America. Oral narratives, songs and participatory performances transmit knowledge associated with cassava cultivation, fishing and canoe building. Their 2008 inscription followed a 2001 proclamation; neither date marks the beginning of the culture.

Research on women estate workers links their withdrawal from plantation labour after apprenticeship to abusive working conditions. Growing and selling provision crops offered an alternative. This helps explain emancipation through choices about work and household survival, alongside the legal dates that changed labourers’ status.

Arrowroot cultivation and starch processing have supported families in northern and northeastern Saint Vincent, particularly Indigenous communities. A 2019 design brief describes the crop’s dense roots and leafy cover as useful on loose volcanic soils, while noting that unusually heavy rain could still erode fields. Agricultural knowledge here involves both production and care for sloping land.

The same brief describes an existing factory where grinding had to pause while starch settled under gravity. Its proposed replacement aimed to connect processing more effectively with pulverizing and packing. The document reveals how growers’ livelihoods depended on factory maintenance and processing capacity; the proposal alone does not prove the new plant was operating.

Craftworkers use bamboo, banana fibre, palm leaves and grasses for baskets, mats, hats and other objects. Wood carving, clothing, steel pans and goatskin drums also appear among documented local industries. These practices combine knowledge of materials with the needs of households, performers and markets.

During the 2020 to 2021 eruption, the UWI Seismic Research Centre, Montserrat Volcano Observatory and local monitoring staff combined earthquake records, gas measurements, cameras and ground movement data. Expanding the instrument network made changes in activity easier to observe. Scientists interpreted several kinds of evidence together rather than relying on a single warning signal.

On 8 April 2021, increased activity prompted a red alert and evacuation before explosions began the next day. The researchers emphasize preparedness, communication and uncertainty in forecasting. The achievement was a coordinated response involving scientists, authorities and residents, with decisions made before the eventual course of the eruption was known.

After the eruption, northern residents used photography and community walks to document changes in their surroundings. Participants also helped identify locations for rain gauges and monitored rainfall with scientific support. Their photographs were exhibited in Kingstown and Sandy Bay in 2022, making local experience part of the record of recovery.

Adult suffrage and self-government developed through several institutional changes. The 1951 voting reform was followed by ministers in 1956 and associated statehood in 1969. These dates distinguish broader political participation from full independence, which required another constitutional settlement.

ending.text: Colonial rule ended with independence in 1979, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines continues as a nation. The earlier defeat and deportation of Garifuna communities did not end their culture or ties with the island. Separate map intervals do not represent repeated national extinctions.
